directions: Thompsonii is grown primarily for its bold maple-shaped leaves, heavily mottled and speckled yellow-gold over green from a naturally occurring, cosmetically harmless leaf virus, with orange, dark-veined pendant flowers appearing as a secondary feature through the warm months. The upright, somewhat open shrub benefits from regular pinching to stay full rather than leggy, and shows its brightest variegation with a few hours of direct morning sun followed by afternoon shade. Grow in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil, and expect significant dieback after hard frost, with recovery likely from mulched roots in zone 9 or from container plants overwintered under cover farther north.

common_name: Variegated Trailing Abutilon (Variegated Red Vein Flowering Maple)
directions: This sport of the species adds irregular cream-to-yellow mottling across the small, maple-shaped leaves, giving the same lantern-like red-calyx, yellow-petaled flowers an extra season of visual interest from the foliage alone. The naturally trailing to lax habit suits hanging baskets and cascading over low walls better than upright staking, and flowering is heaviest with steady moisture and light monthly feeding. As with the plain species, expect frost dieback most winters in zone 8, usually followed by resprouting from mulched roots, or grow it in a movable container where winters run colder.

Suntense produces masses of large, open, saucer-shaped mauve-purple flowers in late spring against soft, grey-green, felted vine-shaped leaves, growing quickly into a substantial, somewhat gaunt shrub. It performs best trained against a warm wall where its brittle wood gets wind shelter and the roots sit in consistently free-draining soil, since winter wet is the most common cause of loss. Because it is a sterile hybrid it must be propagated by cuttings rather than seed, and plants are often relatively short-lived, needing replacement after a decade or so of vigorous growth.

common_name: White Charm Abutilon (White Suntense Flowering Maple)
directions: White Charm is the pure white-flowered selection of the vitifolium x ochsenii hybrid, carrying the same large, open saucer blooms as the mauve-flowered form but in clean white against grey-green, felted, vine-shaped foliage. Growth is fast and somewhat gaunt, so it is usually trained flat against a warm, sheltered wall where its brittle branches get wind protection. Give it free-draining soil in full sun, and expect this fast-growing shrub to be relatively short-lived, typically needing replacement after roughly a decade.

Despite the common name Swedish ivy, this trailing South African species is unrelated to true ivy and is grown for its glossy, rounded, scalloped leaves on fleshy, fast-cascading stems that root wherever they touch soil. Small white-to-pale-lavender flower spikes appear occasionally but are secondary to the dense, trailing foliage display, which has made it a classic hanging-basket and office houseplant for generations. It thrives in bright indirect light to partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and is frost-tender, best grown as a houseplant or container specimen outside zones 10-11.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

directions: Vick's Plant carries thick, velvety, rounded leaves that are green above and deep purple beneath, releasing a strong medicinal, menthol-like scent reminiscent of vapor rub whenever the foliage is brushed or bruised, which earned it the common name. It forms a low, spreading mound or trailing mat topped occasionally by small blue flower spikes, and is grown mainly as a sensory and textural foliage plant in herb gardens, hanging baskets, and warm-climate groundcover plantings rather than for culinary use. Give it well-drained soil and moderate water, since soggy conditions quickly rot the fleshy stems, and treat it as tender, overwintering cuttings indoors outside zones 9-11.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: This twining Western Australian evergreen threads itself through a trellis or neighboring shrub and opens nodding, bell-shaped blue flowers from late spring into autumn. It handles bright dappled shade under open woodland canopy as well as it does part sun, and tends to flower and fruit less heavily if pushed into deep shade. Light, well-drained soil and occasional deep watering keep it tidy; prune hard after flowering to prevent it from smothering companions, since it self-layers readily where stems touch soil.

Native to the jarrah and karri woodlands of southwestern Australia, this wiry twiner scrambles along the ground or up through open shrub canopy and carries clusters of red-and-black pea flowers through winter and spring. It is naturally a dappled-shade understory plant and resents being stripped of that cover, performing poorly in reflected full sun. Once established it needs very little supplemental water, and light, gritty, well-drained soil mimics its native leaf-litter habitat best.

Rediscovered as a single wild plant on New Zealand's Three Kings Islands and propagated from it ever since, this vigorous evergreen climber carries glossy leathery leaves and hangs clusters of waxy, cream-to-pink tubular flowers in late winter and early spring. In its native forest understory it climbs tree trunks in deep, constant shade and keeps that same preference in cultivation, flowering reliably even on a shaded wall or beneath tree canopy. Give it rich, moisture-retentive soil and shelter from hard frost and drying wind.

A lesser-grown relative of the more familiar Holboellia coriacea and H. latifolia, this Chinese woodland twiner carries leathery evergreen leaflets and small, faintly sweet-scented purplish-white flowers in spring, occasionally followed by edible sausage-shaped purple fruit after a warm summer. It is a true woodland-margin vine, flowering and fruiting best with filtered light rather than open sun, and tolerates fairly deep shade once its root system is established. Consistent moisture and a humus-rich soil replicate the forest-floor conditions it comes from.

Known as kaihua to Maori, this New Zealand forest-margin climber starts out as a wiry, small-leaved juvenile tangle before transforming into a vigorous twining vine with larger leaves and clusters of small, sweetly fragrant cream flowers in summer. It is adapted to the broken light of native bush edges and performs best with morning sun or all-day dappled shade rather than hot, exposed sites. Keep soil consistently moist and mulched, and give it something substantial to climb since mature growth becomes quite woody and heavy.
sources: Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture

directions: This dioecious Australian woodland clematis scrambles through understory shrubs and small trees along wet forest margins, opening cream-white starry flowers in spring that give way to fluffy, silvery seed heads on female plants. Unlike many showier hybrid clematis, it is genuinely at home in the broken light of a forest edge and does not need strong sun to flower well. Cool, shaded, humus-rich soil at the root zone with the top growth allowed to reach toward brighter gaps suits it best, following the classic clematis rule of shaded feet and a sunnier head.

A broad-leaved understory shrub from the Himalayan foothills, this Luculia opens large rounded clusters of fragrant pink flowers in autumn and into winter, a season when few other shade shrubs are blooming. In its native forest margins it grows beneath a broken canopy and resents hot, exposed afternoon sun, which scorches the big soft leaves and shortens bloom time. Give it rich, well-drained soil, steady moisture, and shelter from drying wind, and expect it to need winter protection or container culture anywhere colder than the warmest temperate zones.

Renosterbos is the small, wiry, grey-leaved daisy shrub that gives renosterveld vegetation its name and structure, forming dense stands over the fine-textured shale soils of the Western and Eastern Cape. It carries tiny inconspicuous flower heads in autumn and winter rather than showy blooms, so its garden value is architectural and ecological rather than floral. Grow it in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun with minimal summer water, since it is adapted to a long dry season followed by winter rain. Because renosterveld habitat is critically reduced and fragmented, renosterbos is increasingly propagated for restoration plantings as well as low-water indigenous gardens.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica
Red List of South African Plants

directions: Blombos is a tough, wiry-stemmed Asteraceae shrub with narrow, needle-like leaves and clusters of small white to pink everlasting-type flower heads that persist on the plant for months and dry well. It occurs through renosterveld, strandveld, and fynbos margins of the Cape, usually on rocky or shale slopes where little else holds dense cover, and it resprouts readily after fire. In cultivation it wants full sun, lean and fast-draining soil, and little supplemental water once established; it takes hard pruning well and has traditionally been bundled for brush fencing. Its persistent dried flower heads also make it useful in everlasting and dried-flower arrangements.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica
Silverhill Seeds (Cape Town indigenous seed specialists)

directions: This low Cape shrub carries finely divided, silvery-grey, aromatic foliage that looks almost fern-like, topped from late winter into spring with small, bright golden-yellow daisy flower heads. It grows naturally on rocky, shale-influenced slopes at the boundary of renosterveld and fynbos in the southwestern Cape, where it needs sharp drainage and resents being kept wet. Full sun and lean, gritty soil keep it compact and floriferous, and a light trim after flowering maintains its neat mounded shape. It is grown mainly as a foliage and rock-garden plant by South African indigenous-plant enthusiasts.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica

directions: Slangbos is a small, heath-like Cape shrub with slender, silvery, needle-fine leaves and tiny pale flower heads that give the whole plant a soft, feathery, silver-grey appearance. It is a common and often dominant component of renosterveld, especially on degraded or grazed shale slopes, where it is notably unpalatable to livestock and can increase under heavy grazing pressure. In a dry garden setting it provides fine-textured silver foliage contrast and needs only full sun, lean well-drained soil, and minimal irrigation. It is used in renosterveld restoration plantings as an easy, resilient pioneer shrub.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica

directions: Rooigras is a warm-season tussock grass that forms a dominant grassy layer through renosterveld and much of southern African grassland, turning a distinctive reddish-orange color as it cures in late summer and autumn. The same species is grown in Australia as kangaroo grass, where it has become a popular low-water native lawn and meadow grass. It wants full sun and tolerates poor, shallow soils, responding well to occasional fire or mowing that mimics its natural disturbance regime. Established tussocks are long-lived and useful for erosion control, grazing, and naturalistic meadow plantings.

This small cormous geophyte of Cape strandveld and renosterveld lowlands produces grass-like leaves and starry, satin-pink to purple flowers with a yellow throat in winter and early spring, closing again each afternoon. It needs a distinct wet-winter, dry-summer cycle, going fully dormant underground once the dry season arrives. Plant corms shallowly in full sun and well-drained soil and withhold water during summer dormancy to avoid rot. Outside its native range it has also naturalized along roadsides and pastures in parts of Australia and California, a sign of how readily its corms establish and multiply.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica
Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Western Australia — weed profile

directions: A close relative of the better-known Cape snow bush, this Eriocephalus species is centered on the sandy strandveld and coastal renosterveld margins of the Western Cape rather than the fynbos proper. Its fine, grey-green, camphor-scented foliage and small white woolly-seeded flower heads give it the same ornamental and aromatic appeal as its fynbos cousin, while its coastal-sand origin makes it notably tolerant of wind, salt, and dune-type soils. Grow it in full sun and fast-draining sandy soil with little irrigation once established, trimming lightly after its main winter bloom. It is used much like other wild rosemaries, as a landscape foliage shrub and occasional culinary substitute for rosemary.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) — PlantZAfrica
University of Cape Town — Fynbos and Strandveld Flora

directions: Coiron blanco is one of the dominant tussock grasses of the Patagonian steppe in Argentina and Chile, forming pale, dense clumps across vast expanses of cold, windswept, semi-arid grassland. It is extremely frost and wind tolerant, adapted to a short growing season and low, erratic rainfall, and it provides key forage and erosion control in rangeland settings. In cultivation it serves as a hardy ornamental or restoration bunchgrass for cold, dry, exposed sites, needing full sun and sharp drainage but almost no supplemental irrigation once rooted in. It is slow to establish from seed and benefits from division of existing tussocks where available.
sources: Instituto Nacional de Tecnologia Agropecuaria (INTA), Argentina

directions: Known locally as coiron amargo, this needlegrass (long treated under the genus Stipa) is one of the most widespread tussock grasses of the Patagonian steppe, covering enormous areas of cold desert in Argentina and southern Chile. Its narrow, bitter-tasting leaves are grazed sparingly by sheep and guanaco, and its deep, fibrous roots help stabilize thin, wind-eroded steppe soils. It is essentially a plant for cold, dry, rocky or sandy ground in full sun, needing no irrigation and no soil amendment once established. It is used primarily in rangeland and steppe-restoration contexts rather than mainstream ornamental horticulture, with seed collected mainly for revegetation work.
sources: Instituto Nacional de Tecnologia Agropecuaria (INTA), Argentina

directions: Neneo is a dense, rounded, intricately spiny shrub of the carrot family that forms low grey-green mounds across the Patagonian steppe, where it is one of the most recognizable and widespread woody plants. Its tangle of rigid, thorny branchlets deters grazing animals, and the plant copes with the region's relentless wind, cold, and aridity by growing low, compact, and tough, with small yellow umbel flowers appearing among the spines in late spring and summer. Specialist rock-garden and alpine growers occasionally cultivate it for its sculptural cushion form. Give it full sun, gritty well-drained soil, and no winter wet.
sources: Universidad Nacional de la Patagonia San Juan Bosco

directions: This tight, glossy, apple-green cushion plant carpets rocky ground across the Patagonian steppe and adjacent Andean foothills, forming dense mats of tiny overlapping leaves studded with small yellow-green flowers in summer. Long sold in the alpine and rock-garden trade under its older name Bolax gummifera, it is prized for the extreme neatness of its mat, which looks almost artificial in its uniformity. It prefers gritty, sharply drained soil, full sun to light shade, and even moisture without waterlogging, and resents hot, humid summers. It is propagated by division of established mats rather than seed in most garden settings.

Quilimbay is a rigid, grey-spined shrub of the Patagonian steppe whose clusters of tubular orange-red flowers at the branch tips make it one of the most visually striking plants of an otherwise muted landscape, flowering through the austral summer. It is adapted to extreme wind exposure, cold winters, and a short, dry growing season, surviving on thin, rocky, alkaline soils where few other woody plants persist. In cultivation, mainly among Argentine and Chilean native-plant enthusiasts, it needs full sun, sharp drainage, and minimal water once rooted. Its tough, spiny architecture also makes it useful as an informal barrier planting in steppe-climate gardens.

Mata guanaco is a low, densely branched pea-family cushion shrub of the Patagonian steppe that smothers itself in brilliant red-orange flowers in late spring, a striking contrast against its tight grey-green mound of tiny leaves. It survives some of the harshest conditions in Patagonia, tolerating extreme wind, cold, and nutrient-poor rocky or gravelly soils with very little moisture. It is grown in a very limited way by alpine and rock-garden specialists outside South America, who prize it for its cushion habit and intense flower color but find it slow and challenging to establish. Full sun, excellent drainage, and patience are essential, since plants may take years to reach flowering size from seed.

Pichi is an upright, heath-like evergreen shrub native to the drier steppe margins and foothill country of Patagonia and the Andes, with scale-like leaves on slender green stems that give it a heather-like texture. In spring it produces an abundance of narrow, tubular white to pale lavender flowers that cover the whole plant, and its foliage is traditionally brewed into a bitter diuretic tea in Chilean and Argentine folk medicine. It needs full sun and sharply drained, lean soil, tolerating considerable cold and drought but resenting heavy, waterlogged ground. In cultivation outside South America it is grown mainly by specialist shrub collectors for its unusual texture and reliable spring bloom.

Paramela is a resinous, intensely aromatic shrub of the Patagonian steppe and forest-steppe transition zone, its small compound leaves coated in sticky, fragrant resin that gives off a strong herbal scent when brushed or crushed. Small yellow pea-like flowers appear in summer, and the dried leafy twigs are traditionally steeped as a folk-medicine tea in Patagonian Argentina and Chile for digestive and respiratory complaints. It thrives in poor, rocky, well-drained soil under intense sun and cold winters, needing no irrigation once established. It is harvested both from wild stands and small-scale cultivated plantings for the regional herbal tea trade.
sources: Universidad Nacional del Comahue — Patagonian ethnobotany studies
